newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's Nov c/a deficit surges to $1.87 billion.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's Nov c/a deficit surges to $1.87 billion.

text.p: South Korea's current account deficit expanded to $1.87 billion in November from $179.6 million a year earlier, preliminary figures released by the Bank of Korea (BOK) showed on Monday.
Note: figures are in millions of US dollars
A central bank official said the bank saw this year's current account deficit swelling to over $22 billion from its earlier forecast of about $21.5 billion.
The deficit for calendar 1995 was $8.95 billion.

"Traditionally, we've seen strong exports at the year end. But that's unlikely to be the case this year with labour strikes hindering exports during the last week of this month," said Paeng Dong-joon, director of the central bank's statistics division. "At this point, the current account deficit is seen well above $22 billion for the year," he said.
The deficit was $21.6 billion for the first 11 months of this year, compared with $8.6 billion a year ago, he said.
The central bank said the widening deficit in November was mostly due to continuing exports slowdown and rising imports.
Free-on-board exports grew a mere 2.5 percent year-on-year to $11.57 billion in November, while imports rose 15.1 percent to $12.76 billion, it said.

Customs-cleared imports of raw materials rose 6.4 percent November, falling sharply from a 29.4 percent growth a year earlier. Imports of food and consumer goods gained 18.7 percent in November, compared with a 21.4 percent rise a year ago.
Letters of credit received in November dropped 3.5 percent to $5.53 billion from a year ago. Import licence issues also fell 7.3 percent to $12.1 billion, the central bank said.

The expansion in the invisible trade deficit was due mainly to rises in travel and transportation expenses. The travel deficit rose to $183.1 million in November from $65.5 million a year earlier, the figures showed.
"Travel expenses are getting out of hand. This is the area where we should try to cut down," said Paeng.
